kurz: How purchasing power is measured, why the real interest rate is the meaningful figure and who benefits from rising prices.

bloecke.md:
In August 2026 the German consumer price index stood at 125.8 points (base 2020 = 100). A basket of goods and services that cost a hundred euros in 2020 therefore now costs around €126. Of €100 that has been sitting in a current account since 2020, €79.49 of purchasing power is left. Around a fifth of the purchasing power has been lost without any amount ever being debited.

Inflation reduces the value of money without taking anything out of the account. The balance stays the same, but you can buy less with it.

The second figure from the same month was 2.9%. This is the inflation rate, meaning the change in the index compared with the same month of the previous year. The inflation rate and the price level are often confused. If the rate falls from 8.8% (October 2022) to 2.9%, prices merely rise more slowly; the price level does not fall as a result. It can only fall if the rate is negative. The last time Germany had such deflation as an annual average was in 1986, at minus 0.1%; the last individual months with a negative rate were in the second half of 2020.

bloecke.unter: Annual averages of the consumer price index, up to 1991 for the former West German territory and from 1992 for Germany as a whole; the series has a break at this point. On average the rate was just under 2.5%, and in around three quarters of the years it was between 0% and 4%. Larger swings are confined to a few phases and were mostly caused by energy prices.

bloecke.md:
## Measuring the price level

The Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) collects several hundred thousand individual prices every month and weights them using the [[weighting scheme]], the spending pattern of an average household. Housing and energy carry the most weight; a train ticket counts for less than rent. Every few years the index is moved to a new base, most recently to 2020 = 100. Such rebasings change the published rates retroactively. For December 2022 the headlines at the time reported 8.6%; in today's series the figure is 8.1%. The difference is due solely to the new base.

Three measures need to be kept apart. The [[Consumer price index (CPI)|consumer price index]] (CPI) is the national measure of the Federal Statistical Office. The [[Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP)|HICP]] (Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices) is calculated according to uniform European rules and is the measure the ECB is guided by. In August 2026 it stood at 3.2% for the euro area, while the German CPI stood at 2.9%. [[Core inflation]] leaves out energy and food, because their prices fluctuate strongly and hardly respond to monetary policy. In August 2026 it was 2.4%. Over the medium term the ECB aims for an HICP rate of 2% and regards this target as symmetric. A single monthly figure of 3.2% therefore does not yet count as missing the target, whereas a trend lasting several years does. The projection of 10 September 2026 expects 3.0% for 2026, 2.5% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028.

bloecke.md:
## Perceived and measured inflation

The table shows why your own perception is almost always above the official rate. The index represents an average household that does not exist in this form. For commuters who drive 20,000 kilometres a year, what mattered in August 2026 was above all the 27.7% rise in fuel prices rather than the 2.9% rise in the index. Tenants who have lived in the same flat for eight years barely notice the 1.9% rise in net basic rents, even though rents carry a high weight in the basket of goods. Purchase frequency also plays a part. Prices you see every week, for example for groceries, fuel or coffee, shape perceptions more strongly than the annual insurance bill.

A second point of contention is quality adjustment. If a laptop becomes more expensive and faster at the same time, official statistics strip out part of the price increase as a gain in quality. This procedure is called the hedonic method. Supporters argue that it measures the price per unit of benefit, and that this is the right measure. Critics object that nobody can buy the old quality at the old price and that the rate therefore comes out systematically too low. Both positions are defensible. The only certainty is that the official rate rests on statistical conventions.

The official rate is the relevant figure for contracts, pay negotiations and monetary policy. For your own planning, what matters is how your own budget is made up. For someone who spends 40% of their income on housing and energy and commutes every day, the rise in prices differs from the index, higher or lower depending on how prices develop.

## Nominal and real interest rates

An interest rate on its own says nothing about whether purchasing power is being created. That depends on the gap to inflation. The [[real interest rate]] is usually estimated by subtracting the inflation rate from the nominal interest rate. For small numbers this is sufficient. Division is exact, because the growth in money and the rise in prices combine multiplicatively.

bloecke.erklaerung: The gain in purchasing power follows from the ratio of money growth to price increase and not from their difference (Fisher equation).
variablen: Return in terms of purchasing power
Interest rate or return in euros
Inflation rate for the same period
bloecke.beispiel: 2.00% interest with 2.9% inflation: (1.020 / 1.029) - 1 = -0.87%. The approximation 2.0 - 2.9 gives -0.90%; the difference is negligible. With 10% interest and 8% inflation, the exact value is 1.85% instead of 2.00%. The error of the approximation therefore grows with the level of interest rates.

bloecke.md: In addition, capital income in Germany, as in almost all other countries, is taxed in nominal terms. The flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% plus solidarity surcharge, together 26.375% excluding church tax, applies to the full return in euros, including the part that merely offsets inflation. This means that an illusory gain is taxed as well. In the calculation you therefore always deduct the tax first and only then take inflation into account.

bloecke.md: With 2.9% inflation and the full flat-rate withholding tax rate, an investment must yield 3.94% in nominal terms just to preserve purchasing power. At any lower return, the money slowly loses purchasing power despite earning interest. As long as the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 per person has not been used up, 2.9% is enough for that part of the income. The allowance is the only buffer, and it has been unchanged since 2023.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with constant rates: 100 / (1 + i) to the power of the number of years, start 2026 = €100. At 2.9%, €42.42 remains after 30 years. Over a retirement phase, the difference between 2.0% and 2.9% costs more than is at stake in most debates about fees.

bloecke.md: This curve is decisive for any long-term planning. At 2% inflation, purchasing power halves in 35 years; at 2.9%, in just over 24 years. A household that needs €1,000 a month for living expenses today will need €1,641 in 25 years for the same standard of living at 2%, and €2,044 at 2.9%. Every promise of a fixed nominal amount loses value to the same extent, for example a private pension or the guaranteed maturity payout of a life insurance policy. Company pensions already in payment, by contrast, must as a rule be reviewed by the employer every three years for adjustment to rising prices under Section 16 BetrAVG (Occupational Pensions Act), although the employer may refuse the adjustment if its economic situation is poor. For long-term contracts, whether the amount is fixed in nominal terms or linked to an index therefore matters more than its size.

## Inflation protection in historical comparison

Over very long periods the picture is clear. According to the database of Dimson, Marsh and Staunton, US equities returned 6.6% a year in real terms from 1900 to 2025, long-term bonds 1.6%, the money market 0.5% and gold 1.3%. US inflation over this period was 2.9% a year. Measured worldwide, equities achieved a real 5.2% from 1900 to 2024, bonds 1.7% and the money market 0.5%. The final values make the difference clear. A dollar invested in US equities in 1900 grew to around $124,900 in nominal terms by the end of 2025, or to $3,296 in 1900 purchasing power. The same dollar in the money market reached $1.80 in real terms.

However, these results only hold over very long periods. Equities protect against inflation over decades, but not over individual quarters. In the inflationary period from 1966 to 1981, US equities lost 0.82% a year in real terms, so for sixteen years there was no gain in purchasing power. Gold is regarded as an inflation hedge, but in 13 of the 28 years with US inflation above 3% it made a real loss.

bloecke.unter: USA, 1900 to 2025, after deducting inflation of 2.9% p.a.; in nominal terms the figures were 9.8% for equities, 4.6% for bonds and 3.4% for the money market. Source: UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook 2026 (Dimson/Marsh/Staunton).

bloecke.md: Investors who put money into equities or bonds in 2022 because inflation was 8% were taking a risk. That year both asset classes fell at the same time, and ten-year German federal bonds lost around a fifth of their market value. Protection against inflation is a finding about long periods. It is not a suitable reason for reacting to headlines.

punkte: Borrowers with a fixed rate and a long fixed-rate period
The state as the largest debtor in the economy
Incomes that catch up through indexation or collective agreements
Holders of inflation-linked bonds, provided inflation turns out higher than was priced in at purchase
The tax authorities, as long as the tax scale is not adjusted
Any claim fixed in nominal terms: fixed-term deposits, conventional bonds, home savings balances (Bausparguthaben)
Fixed private pensions and company pensions whose adjustments lag behind rising prices
Savers facing a negative real interest rate, whose purchasing power falls slowly but steadily
Borrowers at the end of the fixed-rate period, when the loan is renewed at higher rates
Taxpayers who pay tax on nominal gains without any real increase

bloecke.md:
An outstanding debt of €100,000 with a ten-year fixed-rate period remains a debt of €100,000 in nominal terms for ten years. Measured in today's purchasing power, at 2.9% inflation it is worth only €75,136 at the end (100,000 / 1.029 to the power of 10).

For the borrower to benefit from this, two conditions must be met. First, the interest rate must be fixed. When the fixed-rate period ends, the loan is renewed at the rates then applicable, and high inflation and high interest rates rarely occur separately. Second, your own income must rise with inflation. If prices rise but wages do not, the erosion of the debt does the borrower no good.

## Bracket creep

The German income tax scale is progressive, which means that the marginal tax rate rises with income. If a salary rises exactly in line with the inflation rate, the purchasing power of gross pay stays the same. However, the additional euro is taxed at the higher marginal rate. The average tax rate rises even though nothing has been gained in real terms. This effect is called [[bracket creep]].

Taxable income is €45,000, calculated using the tax scale under Section 32a EStG (Income Tax Act) as applicable for 2026. Income tax amounts to €8,835, the average tax rate is 19.6% and the marginal tax rate is 33.4%.

The salary rises by exactly 2.9% to €46,305. If the tax scale remained unchanged, €9,274 would be due. Tax therefore rises by 4.96%, income by 2.9%. The average rate increases to 20.0%.

After tax, €37,031 now remains instead of €36,165, an increase of 2.40%. With 2.9% inflation, this means around 0.5% less purchasing power in real terms than before, even though the gross salary fully offsets inflation. Social security contributions are not taken into account. Up to the contribution assessment ceiling (Beitragsbemessungsgrenze) they are proportional and do not by themselves cause bracket creep.

bloecke.titel: Tax scale adjustments and fixed amounts
bloecke.md:
Because this effect is well known, the legislator raises the thresholds of the tax scale almost every year. For 2026 the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag) is €12,348, the 42% rate starts at €69,879 and the 45% rate at €277,826. If the increase matches inflation, bracket creep is offset. If it is smaller, a remainder is left.

Other amounts are not adjusted at all. The saver's allowance has remained unchanged at €1,000 per person since 2023, and the flat-rate withholding tax makes no adjustment for inflation. Both therefore become stricter with every year of inflation without any law being changed.

Any return figure can be checked on three points: whether it is nominal or real, whether it applies before or after tax, and over what period it is calculated. With these three checks, most advertising claims can be weeded out without any further specialist knowledge.

mitnehmen: Inflation reduces purchasing power without changing the account balance; with the consumer price index at 125.8 in August 2026, a balance from 2020 has lost around a fifth of its purchasing power.
A falling inflation rate only means that prices are rising more slowly; the price level only goes down in deflation, and Germany has almost never had that since 1950.

The meaningful figure is the real return, for which you first deduct tax and then divide by the price increase; at 2.9% inflation and the full flat-rate withholding tax rate, it takes a nominal 3.94% just to preserve purchasing power.

Over decades, equities have delivered a real return, 5.2% a year worldwide since 1900, but in inflationary phases they often failed to do so for years; their protection against inflation only holds in the long term.
Inflation shifts wealth from creditors to debtors and from taxpayers to the tax authorities without any decision or invoice.

begriffe.text: National price index of the Federal Statistical Office with the base 2020 = 100. It measures the price development of a weighted basket of goods. The inflation rate is the change in the index compared with the same month of the previous year.

Harmonised consumer price index calculated according to uniform European rules. The ECB measures its 2% target against the HICP and not against the national CPI, which makes it the relevant measure for monetary policy.
Inflation rate excluding energy and food. It shows broad, slow-moving price pressure, because the excluded goods fluctuate strongly and hardly respond to interest rates.
Weighting of the groups of goods in the price index according to the spending pattern of an average household. It determines how strongly an individual price increase affects the overall rate.

Interest measured in terms of purchasing power, calculated as (1 + nominal interest rate) divided by (1 + inflation rate), minus 1. The common subtraction method is only accurate enough for small rates.

Increase in the real tax burden when incomes rise only because of inflation and the progressive tax scale stays unchanged. The legislator offsets it fully or partly by raising the thresholds of the tax scale every year.
